Tomato_Early_blight.summary: Fungal early blight with concentric leaf lesions and defoliation.
actions: Remove and dispose of heavily infected leaves and crop debris.
Improve spacing and airflow; avoid overhead irrigation and keep foliage dry.
Rotate away from tomato/other solanaceous hosts where practical.
Use a locally registered fungicide only when warranted and strictly according to its label and local extension guidance.
sources: Penn State Extension: Tomato Diseases and Disorders in the Home Garden

Tomato_Late_blight.summary: Late blight can spread rapidly under cool, wet conditions.
actions: Scout frequently and remove infected tissue promptly.
Avoid overhead irrigation; water so leaves dry quickly.
Improve airflow and remove volunteer plants/weeds that increase humidity.
For confirmed outbreaks, use locally registered fungicides according to the current label and extension recommendations; severely infected plants may need destruction.
sources: Penn State Extension: Tomato-Potato Late Blight in the Home Garden

Potato_Late_blight.summary: Late blight affects potato foliage and tubers and is favored by cool, wet weather.
actions: Scout foliage and remove/destroy severely infected plants or cull piles.
Avoid prolonged leaf wetness and improve field airflow.
Use certified healthy seed and manage volunteer potatoes.
Apply only locally registered fungicides according to label and disease forecasting guidance.
sources: Penn State Extension: Tomato-Potato Late Blight in the Home Garden

Potato_Early_blight.summary: Early blight causes dark lesions, often with target-like rings.
actions: Remove infected debris after harvest and rotate crops.
Maintain balanced plant nutrition and irrigation to reduce plant stress.
Avoid prolonged leaf wetness and improve airflow.
Use registered fungicides according to local labels when disease pressure warrants treatment.
sources: Penn State Extension vegetable disease/IPM guidance

Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.summary: Septoria leaf spot produces numerous small spots and can cause defoliation.
actions: Remove lower infected leaves and crop debris.
Avoid overhead irrigation and splash dispersal.
Improve spacing and airflow.
Rotate crops and use registered fungicides according to local recommendations if needed.
sources: Penn State Extension: Scouting and Identifying Tomato Diseases

Tomato_Bacterial_spot.summary: Bacterial spot produces small water-soaked or dark lesions and spreads with splashing water.
actions: Use clean seed/transplants and avoid handling wet plants.
Reduce leaf wetness and water splash.
Remove severely affected debris and sanitize tools.
For chemical control, use only products registered locally and follow the current label/extension guidance.
sources: Penn State Extension: Scouting and Identifying Tomato Diseases

Pepper__bacterial_spot.summary: Bacterial spot of pepper causes leaf and fruit lesions.
actions: Use clean seed and transplants.
Avoid working plants when foliage is wet.
Reduce splash irrigation and improve airflow.
Remove infected debris and follow locally registered bacterial disease control guidance.
sources: Penn State Extension tomato/vegetable bacterial disease scouting guidance

Peach__bacterial_spot.summary: Bacterial spot affects leaves and fruit, especially under warm wet conditions.
actions: Maintain orchard sanitation and remove badly affected material.
Promote airflow through appropriate pruning.
Avoid unnecessary leaf wetness.
Use only locally registered bactericides/fungicides according to the current label and extension advice.
sources: Penn State Extension plant disease management principles

Apple_scab.summary: Apple scab causes olive-to-brown lesions and can affect leaves and fruit.
actions: Remove fallen infected leaves where practical to reduce overwintering inoculum.
Prune for airflow and faster drying.
Choose resistant cultivars when establishing new trees.
Use locally registered fungicides according to label and disease-risk forecasts.

Apple_black_rot.summary: Black rot can cause leaf spots, limb cankers and fruit rot.
actions: Remove mummified fruit and dead/cankered wood.
Prune to improve airflow and reduce dead tissue reservoirs.
Avoid wounding trees and manage orchard sanitation.
Use registered fungicides only when recommended locally and according to label.

Grape_black_rot.summary: Black rot produces leaf spots and dark fruit rot.
actions: Remove mummified berries and infected debris.
Train/prune vines to improve sunlight and airflow.
Scout regularly during wet periods.
Use locally registered fungicides according to label and disease forecasts.

Grape_leaf_blight.summary: Leaf blight causes necrotic foliage and may reduce canopy health.
actions: Remove infected debris and improve canopy airflow.
Avoid prolonged leaf wetness.
Scout regularly and remove severely affected tissue.
Use registered fungicides only under local recommendations and label directions.

Corn_(maize)_Northern_Leaf_Blight.summary: Northern leaf blight causes elongated gray-green to tan lesions.
actions: Plant resistant hybrids where available.
Rotate crops and manage infected residue where practical.
Scout during humid/wet periods.
Use fungicides only where economically justified and registered locally.
sources: University/extension integrated corn disease management principles

Corn_(maize)_Common_Rust.summary: Common rust produces rust-colored pustules on leaves.
actions: Prefer resistant hybrids where suitable.
Scout regularly and assess disease progression.
Maintain balanced crop management to avoid unnecessary stress.
Follow local extension thresholds before using a registered fungicide.
sources: University/extension integrated corn disease management principles

Squash_Powdery_mildew.summary: Powdery mildew appears as white powdery growth on leaves.
actions: Improve spacing and airflow.
Avoid excessive shade and prolonged humidity where possible.
Remove badly infected leaves when practical.
Use resistant varieties and locally registered fungicides according to label when warranted.

Tomato_Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider_m.summary: Two-spotted spider mites are a mite pest associated with stippling and webbing.
actions: Inspect leaf undersides with a hand lens.
Reduce plant stress and dusty conditions; maintain appropriate irrigation.
Conserve predatory mites and other beneficial organisms where possible.
Use a registered miticide only when monitoring shows treatment is warranted and follow the label.
sources: Penn State Extension: Tomato Production / IPM scouting
